directions.description: Gödel showed self-reference breaks completeness, but what if self-referential proofs are not paradoxes but VALID mathematical objects? Develop a proof theory where proofs can reference their own structure — a proof of theorem T can contain a subproof that assumes T as a hypothesis, forming a circular dependency that is resolved through a fixed-point construction. Conjecture: Non-well-founded proofs form a convergent fixed point under a natural topolog: the space of proof trees with the tree topology is a Scott domain, and self-referential proofs correspond to infinite chains whose lub is a valid proof. A proof that references itself is like a recursive function: it converges if the self-reference occurs at a strictly smaller ordinal. Test: formalize non-well-founded proof trees as coinductive types in Lean 4, prove that the proof of 'P implies P' by assuming P is a valid non-well-founded proof with ordinal height 1, and show that the liar sentence 'this statement is unprovable' is NOT a valid non-well-founded proof because its ordinal height is undefined. Impact: turns the liar paradox from a bug into a feature — self-referential proofs are a new class of mathematical object with their own consistency conditions.
directions.proof_strategy: Define NWFP (non-well-founded proofs) as coinductive types: a proof is a tree where children are proofs, but cycles are allowed as long as each cycle has decreasing ordinal rank. Define ordinal height: oh(P) = sup{oh(Q)+1 : Q is a subproof of P}. A NWFP is valid if oh(P) is a well-defined ordinal. Prove consistency: if NWFP proves False, then oh(False) < oh(False), contradiction. Prove completeness: every true Pi_1 sentence has a NWFP of finite height. Test: formalize in Lean 4 and verify the P-implies-P example.
directions.title: Non-Well-Founded Proofs: Proofs That Reference Themselves

directions.description: The integers Z live on a line, but what happens to arithmetic on a curved space? Define hyperbolic integers Z_H as the set of points in the Poincaré disk that are images of Z under a discrete subgroup Gamma of PSL(2,R). Define hyperbolic primes as the vertices of the tessellation induced by Gamma, and hyperbolic addition/multiplication via the group action. Conjecture: Z_H has unique factorization into hyperbolic primes, and the hyperbolic prime number theorem holds: the number of hyperbolic primes in a hyperbolic disk of radius R is asymptotic to R^2 / (2 log R). The hyperbolic zeta function zeta_H(s) = sum_{n in Z_H, |n|_H > 0} 1/|n|_H^{2s} satisfies a functional equation and has zeros only on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2. Test: compute zeta_H(s) for the modular group Gamma = PSL(2,Z) and verify that the first 100 zeros lie on Re(s) = 1/2. Impact: number theory on curved spaces — where primes are geometric objects and the Riemann Hypothesis might be PROVABLE.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Z_H as the orbit of 0 under Gamma = PSL(2,Z) acting on the Poincaré disk. Define |n|_H as the hyperbolic distance from the origin. Prove Z_H is a discrete subset of the disk. Define the hyperbolic zeta function zeta_H(s) = sum 1/|n|_H^{2s} and prove it converges for Re(s) > 1. Prove the functional equation zeta_H(s) = pi^{s-1/2} Gamma((1-s)/2)/Gamma(s/2) zeta_H(1-s) using Selberg's trace formula. Test: compute first 100 zeros numerically and verify Re(s) = 1/2.
directions.title: Hyperbolic Number Theory: Arithmetic on the Poincaré Disk

directions.description: Conway's surreal numbers are the largest ordered field, containing every real number and infinitely many infinities and infinitesimals. But what if a surreal number could be in SUPERPOSITION — simultaneously equal to multiple values until observed? Define quantum surreal numbers as surreal-valued quantum states: |psi> = sum_i alpha_i |No_i> where No_i are surreal numbers and alpha_i are complex amplitudes. Conjecture: The quantum surreal field Q(No) is a non-Archimedean quantum field where the spectral theorem extends: every self-adjoint operator on a quantum surreal Hilbert space has a spectral decomposition into surreal-valued projections. The key insight is that infinitesimal surreal numbers provide a natural framework for quantum measurement: the probability of observing |No_i> is not alpha_i^2 (which may be infinitesimal) but the standard part of alpha_i^2. Test: construct the quantum surreal number |psi> = (1/sqrt(2))|0> + (1/sqrt(2))|epsilon> where epsilon is an infinitesimal surreal, and prove that measuring |psi> gives 0 with probability st(1/2) = 1/2 and epsilon with probability st(1/2 * epsilon^2) = 0 — the infinitesimal is unobservable! Impact: a mathematical framework where quantum mechanics and non-Archimedean analysis meet, giving infinitesimal probabilities a rigorous treatment.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Q(No) as the tensor product of the surreal field No with the complex numbers C. Define quantum surreal Hilbert space H_Q(No) as the completion of Q(No)^n with respect to the surreal-valued inner product. Prove the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators on H_Q(No) by transfinite induction on the birthday of the surreal eigenvalues. The key lemma: if A is self-adjoint with surreal eigenvalues, then A = integral lambda dE(lambda) where E(lambda) are projections and lambda ranges over surreal numbers up to the birthday of A. Test: construct the 2x2 example and verify measurement probabilities.
directions.title: Quantum Surreal Numbers: Superposition of All Real Numbers

directions.description: Zero-knowledge proofs let you convince someone a statement is true without revealing WHY. Apply this to mathematics: a zero-knowledge proof of a theorem T convinces the verifier that T is provable in PA without revealing any step of the proof. Conjecture: Every theorem provable in Peano Arithmetic has a zero-knowledge proof whose communication complexity is polynomial in the length of the theorem statement (not the proof). This follows from the PCP theorem combined with the fact that PA-proofs can be arithmetized. The zero-knowledge protocol: (1) Prover commits to each proof step using a collision-resistant hash. (2) Verifier randomly challenges one proof step. (3) Prover opens that step and shows it follows from the axioms. Repeating O(k) times gives soundness error 2^{-k}. The proof is zero-knowledge because the verifier only sees one random step per challenge. Test: implement a zero-knowledge proof system for propositional tautologies and prove that a verifier learns nothing beyond the validity of the tautology. Impact: mathematicians can certify results without revealing their methods — a mathematical equivalent of sealed-bid auctions for proof strategies.
directions.proof_strategy: Arithmetize PA-proofs: encode each proof step as a polynomial equation over a finite field F_p. Apply the PCP theorem: every NP statement has a probabilistically checkable proof of constant query complexity. Convert the PCP to zero-knowledge using the Fiat-Shamir heuristic: the prover commits to the PCP oracle, the verifier sends a random challenge, and the prover responds with a proof that is zero-knowledge by the hiding property of the commitment. Prove soundness: a cheating prover must fool the verifier with probability at most 2^{-k}. Prove zero-knowledge: the simulator can generate indistinguishable transcripts without the proof. Test: implement for propositional resolution proofs of length up to 1000.
directions.title: Zero-Knowledge Theorem Proving: I Can Prove Fermat's Last Theorem Without Showing You the Proof

directions.description: Borges' Library of Babel contains every possible 410-page book — approximately 25^{1312000} volumes. The library is finite but vast beyond comprehension. Formalize the Library as the set of all strings over a 25-symbol alphabet of length 1312000. Conjecture: The probability that a random volume contains a meaningful proof of a given theorem T is approximately |T| * 25^{-k} where |T| is the length of T and k is the proof complexity of T. Moreover, the Library contains a universal catalog — a single volume that encodes the location of every other volume — and this catalog can be found in polynomial time using a variant of the de Bruijn sequence construction. The deepest question: does the Library contain its own complete catalog? By a diagonal argument, no single volume can encode all volumes (since 25^{1312000} > 1312000 * log_2(25^{1312000})). But a DISTRIBUTED catalog spanning N volumes can encode the entire Library if N > 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_2(25)). Test: compute the exact probability of finding a valid Lean 4 proof of a specific theorem in the Library. Construct a de Bruijn-based catalog for a mini-Library with alphabet size 4 and book length 16. Impact: the mathematics of universal information spaces — every possible text exists, but finding meaning requires a guide.
directions.proof_strategy: Define B = {0,...,24}^{1312000} as the Library. Compute |B| = 25^{1312000}. Define the meaning probability P(T) = sum_{b in B: b contains proof of T} 1/|B|. Prove P(T) >= |T| * 25^{-k(T)} where k(T) is the Kolmogorov complexity of T. Construct a distributed catalog using de Bruijn sequences: encode each volume's address as a substring of a de Bruijn sequence B(25, m) for m = ceil(log_{25}(1312000)). Prove the catalog requires N >= 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_{25}(2)) volumes. Test: implement the mini-Library with alphabet 4, book length 16, and compute meaning probabilities.
directions.title: The Library of Babel: Combinatorics of the Universal Library

directions.description:
# Future Directions — Congruence Rigidity of Sums of Squares

This cycle established that the entries of an integer right triangle are forced into
strong divisibility patterns — one leg is a multiple of three, the legs jointly carry a
factor of four, one entry is a multiple of five — and that a four-dimensional right
"box" (a solution of `a² + b² + c² = d²`) is even more rigid: at most one of its three
spatial edges can be odd. We also pinned down exactly which whole numbers can serve as a
leg. These findings point to several bold, testable conjectures.

## 1. The correct modulus for a power of two grows with the power
**Conjecture.** In any solution of `a² + b² = c²`, the two-adic valuation of the leg
product `a·b` is governed one level deeper than naive reduction suggests: deciding
whether `2^k` divides `a·b` is a question about residues modulo `2^{k+1}`, never modulo
`2^k`.
*The key insight is* that a difference of two odd squares is always divisible by eight,
so each additional factor of two in the product must be certified one binary place
further out than one would guess. *Why now?* Having isolated the exact `mod 8`
obstruction behind the factor of four, we can test the pattern mechanically for `k = 3,
4, 5` and either confirm a clean "shift-by-one" law or expose its first exception.

## 2. A universal super-divisor for higher-dimensional right figures
**Conjecture.** For every dimension `r`, solutions of `x₁² + ⋯ + x_r² = y²` obey a single
universal divisibility law: there is a constant `D(r)`, depending only on `r`, such that
`D(r)` divides the product `x₁·x₂·⋯·x_r` for *every* solution, and `D(r)` is the largest
such constant.
*The key insight is* that reduction to a finite residue ring turns "for all solutions"
into a finite, decidable statement, so the optimal constant `D(r)` is computable and
should grow in a structured (conjecturally multiplicative-over-primes) way. *Why now?*
The three-dimensional case already yields `4 ∣ x₁x₂x₃`; comparing it against the planar
constant `12` suggests a dimension-indexed sequence worth charting and predicting.

## 3. Parity collapse in higher dimensions
**Conjecture.** As the number of squared terms increases, the number of edges permitted to
be odd stays uniformly bounded: in `x₁² + ⋯ + x_r² = y²` at most three of the `x_i` can be
odd, regardless of `r`.
*The key insight is* that the sum of squares equals the count of odd terms modulo four,
while a perfect square is `0` or `1` modulo four, capping the admissible odd-count no
matter how many terms are added. *Why now?* We proved the cap is "at most one" in three
dimensions; extending the modular bookkeeping to arbitrary `r` is a self-contained next
step that would reveal whether the cap is truly dimension-independent.

## 4. A sharp threshold characterization of legs in every dimension
**Conjecture.** Just as the whole numbers that are a leg of a right triangle are exactly
those `≥ 3`, in each higher dimension there is a sharp finite threshold above which every
integer appears as an edge of some right figure, and the finitely many exceptions can be
listed explicitly.
*The key insight is* that a single explicit construction, split according to the parity of
the target edge, realizes all sufficiently large values, while the small exceptions are
forced by a factorization that would otherwise require a vanishing edge. *Why now?* The
planar threshold `3` and its sharpness (the failures at `1` and `2`) give a template that
should transfer verbatim to the box equation and beyond.

## 5. Divisibility as a sieve against near-solutions
**Conjecture.** The combined congruence obstructions (`12 ∣ a·b`, `60 ∣ a·b·c`, and their
higher-dimensional analogues) are strong enough that a random integer triple satisfying
them has a positive, computable probability of being genuinely Pythagorean — i.e. the
congruence conditions capture a constant fraction of the "arithmetic mass" of true
solutions.
*The key insight is* that each universal divisor removes a fixed proportion of impostors,
so stacking independent prime-power obstructions multiplies into a sieve of predictable
density. *Why now?* With the exact obstructions in hand for the primes `2, 3, 5`, one can
immediately measure how much of the solution set they explain and calibrate whether a few
more primes suffice to pin down solutions almost completely.
directions.title: That the entries of an integer right triangle are forced

directions.description: For any graph $G$, if $G$ is distance-hereditary, then $G$ is balanced if and and only if $G$ does not contain $\overline{3K_2}$ as an induced subgraph. This formalizes the paper's result that for the class of distance-hereditary graphs, the property of being balanced is equivalent to being $\overline{3K_2}$-free.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem balanced_distance_hereditary_iff_no_3K2_complement (G : Graph) : is_distance_hereditary G ↔ (is_balanced G ∧ is_distance_hereditary G) ↔ (is_distance_hereditary G ∧ ¬ ∃ H ⊆_induced G, H ≅ 3K2_complement)
directions.proof_strategy: The proof involves two directions: (1) Showing that if $G$ contains $\overline{3K_2}$ as an induced subgraph, it cannot be balanced (which is true for any graph). (2) Showing that if $G$ is distance-hereditary and contains no induced $\overline{3K_2}$, then it is balanced. The second part relies on the paper's proof that for distance-hereditary graphs, balancedness is equivalent to being hereditary clique-Helly, and then showing that distance-hereditary graphs are hereditary clique-Helly if and only if they are $\overline{3K_2}$-free.
directions.title: Characterization of Balanced Distance-Hereditary Graphs by the Complement of 3-Matching

directions.description: We conjecture that the finite Chromonic Lemma extends to infinite, locally finite, strongly connected digraphs. Formally, let G be an infinite directed graph that is strongly connected and locally finite, equipped with a real‑valued weight function on its edges and a color‑blending operation satisfying the Color Blend Axiom. If there exists a vertex coloring c : V → Colors such that for every vertex v, c(v) equals the weighted blend of the colors of its out‑neighbors (i.e., c(v) = π_{(u,p)∈Out(v)} p·c(u) ), then c must be constant. This generalizes the paper’s result from finite graphs to infinite ones and highlights the robustness of the underlying combinatorial principle.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
-- Conjecture (Infinite Chromonic Lemma)
 theorem infinite_chromic_lemma {V : Type*} [infinite V] [LocallyFinite V] (G : StrongDigraph V) (w : ∀ (e : G.Edge), ℝ) (c : V → Color) :
   (∀ v, c v = blend (λ u => (w (G.edge v u), c u))) → (∀ v, c v = c (Classical.arbitrary V)) := by
   -- proof outline:
   -- 1. Enumerate finite subgraphs G_n exhausting V.
   -- 2. By the finite Chromonic Lemma, each G_n forces c|_{V_n} constant.
   -- 3. Use an ultralimit of the constants to obtain a global constant.
   -- 4. Show any non‑constant coloring would contradict the Color Blend Axiom.
   -- QED
directions.proof_strategy: Extend the finite proof via a compactness/ultraproduct construction: take an increasing sequence of finite subgraphs exhausting G, apply the finite Chromonic Lemma to obtain constant colorings on each subgraph, then use an ultralimit to build a global coloring satisfying the neighbor‑blend condition. The Color Blend Axiom ensures the limit respects blending, and strong connectivity yields a contradiction unless the coloring is constant. Alternatively, formulate the condition as a fixed‑point equation on the space of colorings and apply a Banach‑type contraction argument using the weights and the axiom.
directions.title: Infinite Color Wheels: No Nontrivial Neighbor‑Blend Colorings

directions.description:
We conjecture an explicit formula for the Jordan canonical form of the image of a regular unipotent element under any finite‑dimensional irreducible polynomial representation of GL₃(ₖ). Let λ = (a,b,c) be a dominant weight with a > b > c. Define d₁ = a‑ b, d₂ = b‑ c, d₃ = a‑ c and the rational function

M(t) = (1‑ t^{d₁+1})(1‑ t^{d₂+1})(1‑ t^{d₃+2}) /
       ((1‑ t^{d₁})(1‑ t^{d₂})(1‑ t^{d₃})).

Write M(t) = Σ_{j≥0} m_j t^j. Then the Jordan canonical form of π_λ(u) (the regular unipotent u ∈ GL₃(ₖ) under the representation π_λ) is the partition whose parts are (j+1) repeated m_j times. In particular the multiplicities m_j satisfy a linear recurrence with characteristic polynomial (1‑ t^{d₁})(1‑ t^{d₂})(1‑ t^{d₃}).
directions.proof_strategy: 1. Use the character formula (Serre) to compute Θ_λ(z) as a rational function. 2. Identify the coefficients a_k of z^k in Θ_λ(z) and relate them to the multiplicities m_j via m_j = a_j ‑ a_{j+2}. 3. Show that the generating function M(t) = Σ m_j t^j equals the rational expression above, which yields a linear recurrence for m_j. 4. Prove non‑≥negativity of m_j (e.g., by interpreting them as Kostka numbers). 5. Use the known fact that Sym^j(u_SL₂) has a single Jordan block of size j+1 to conclude that π_λ(u) has Jordan blocks of size j+1 with multiplicities m_j.
directions.title: Jordan type of regular unipotent image for GL₀ representations

directions.description: We conjecture that the explicit bound $P^+(d)$ from the main theorem is optimal: for every $g\ge 2$, $d\in\{2g+1,2g+2\}$ and the corresponding $P^+(d)$, there exist a non‑zero algebraic integer $\alpha$ and a prime $p=P^+(d)$ (with $p\nmid N_{\mathbb Q(\alpha)/\mathbb Q}(\alpha)$) such that the family $\cC_\alpha\colon y^2 = x^d + \alpha x + t$ is **not** generically ordinary at $p$. In other words, the threshold $p>P^+(d)$ cannot be lowered.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem bound_sharp (g : ℕ) (d : ℕ) (h : d = 2*g + 1 ∨ d = 2*g + 2) :
  ∃ (α : AlgebraicInteger) (p : ℕ),
    α ≠ 0 ∧ p = P_plus d ∧ p ∤ norm α ∧ ¬ IsOrdinaryFamily C_α p :=
  -- Existence of an explicit counterexample (e.g. α = -d, p = P_plus d).
  let α := -d,
      p := P_plus d in
  have hp : p = P_plus d := rfl,
  have hα : α ≠ 0 := by simp,
  have hp_norm : p ∤ norm α := by
    -- Since norm (-d) = (-d)^{[ℚ(α):ℚ]} and p does not divide d for the known cases, this holds.
    exact norm_ne_zero_divide,
  have hnonord : ¬ IsOrdinaryFamily C_α p :=
    -- Direct computation of the Hasse‑Witt matrix over 𝔽_p shows det = 0.
    have det := compute_hasse_witt_det α p,
    have det_zero : det = 0 := by exact known_counterexample,
    exact det_zero,
  exact ⟨α, p, hα, hp_norm, hnonord⟩
directions.proof_strategy: 1. Use the explicit counterexamples constructed by Katz (e.g. $(d,p)=(21,359)$, $(31,839)$, $(51,2399)$) together with a suitable choice of $\alpha$ (take $\alpha=-d$ for the original Katz family) to verify directly that the Hasse‑Witt matrix of the reduction $\cC_\alpha$ modulo $p$ has determinant zero for $p=P^+(d)$. 2. Generalise these computations to arbitrary $d$ by showing that the vanishing pattern of the Hasse‑Witt matrix persists for any $\alpha$ with $p\nmid N_{\mathbb Q(\alpha)/\mathbb Q}(\alpha)$, using the known description of the Cartier‑Manin matrix for hyperelliptic curves in terms of the polynomial $x^d+\alpha x+t$. 3. Conclude that the bound $P^+(d)$ is best possible; any lower bound would be contradicted by these explicit families.
directions.title: Sharpness of the ordinary bound for hyperelliptic families

where q(n) is the number of partitions of n into distinct parts, and σ_odd(i) is the sum of odd divisors of i.

This property is the key motivation for the sheared Witt construction and resolves the obstruction in extending Dieudonné theory to non-perfect rings.

directions.description: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies). Moreover, every non-metrizable space requires at least 3 observers. The intuition: the real topology is what ALL observers agree on, and phantom topologies are what individual observers see. Like quantum mechanics, measurement changes the topology. Test: prove that R with the standard topology is the intersection of the lower limit topology and the upper limit topology (2 observers). Prove that the Zariski topology on R^2 requires at least 3 observers. Impact: a new notion of topology where the space itself depends on the observer — the mathematical formalization of 'reality depends on the observer'.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a phantom topology as a function T: O -> Top(X) from a set of observers to topologies on X. Define the intersection topology T_cap = intersection of all T(o). Prove: every second-countable T_0 space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with |O| = 2. Proof: for a basis {B_n}, define T(o1) as the topology generated by {B_n : n odd} union {X} and T(o2) by {B_n : n even} union {X}. Then T_cap = tau. Prove non-metrizable spaces need >= 3 observers: the Zariski topology on R^2 cannot be written as the intersection of two first-countable topologies. Test: verify the R example and construct the 3-observer phantom representation for the Zariski topology.
directions.title: Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them

directions.description: A vampire number is a composite number v with an even number of digits that can be factizedd as v = x * y where x and y together have the same digits as v. The smallest is 1260 = 21 * 60. But vampire numbers are just the beginning. Define: (1) Werewolf numbers: v = x * y where x and y share exactly one digit with v. (2) Ghost numbers: v = x * y where v has NO digits in common with x or y. (3) Zombie numbers: v = x * y where x and y are both prime (these violate the definition but exist — 125460 = 204 * 615 = 246 * 510, where both factorizations involve a prime and a composite). Conjecture: The density of vampire numbers in [10^{2n}, 10^{2n+1}] approaches 1/sqrt(n) as n -> infinity. Every even-length interval [10^{2k}, 10^{2k+2}] contains at least one vampire number. Ghost numbers have density 0 — they become vanishingly rare as the number of digits increases. Test: enumerate all vampire, werewolf, ghost, and zombie numbers up to 10^8. Prove the density conjecture by counting valid digit permutations. Impact: a playful but genuine number theory of arithmetic creatures — combinatorial digit problems that are easy to state but may be as hard as factoring.
directions.proof_strategy: Define vampire numbers formally: v is a vampire number iff v has 2n digits and there exist x, y each with n digits such that v = x*y and the multiset of digits of v equals the union of digits of x and y. Count the number of digit arrangements: for a 2n-digit number with distinct digits, there are C(2n, n) * n! * n! possible fang pairs, so the expected number of fang pairs is C(2n, n) * (n!)^2 / 10^{2n} = C(2n,n) / 10^n ~ 1/sqrt(n). Prove existence in every interval by constructing explicit vampire numbers using the formula 1260 * 10^{2k} for k >= 0. Test: enumerate up to 10^8.
directions.title: Vampire Numbers and Other Numerical Monsters: A Bestiary of Arithmetic Oddities

directions.description: The Fibonacci sequence is defined by F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n-1) and converges to the golden ratio. Define the ANTI-Fibonacci sequence: A(n+1) is the smallest positive integer that is NOT equal to A(n) + A(n-1). The sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ... (each term avoids being the sum of the two previous terms). Conjecture: The anti-Fibonacci sequence A(n) grows as A(n) ~ n^2/4, and the ratio A(n)/n^2 converges to 1/4. More precisely, A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1). The sequence avoids the golden ratio entirely — the ratio A(n+1)/A(n) does NOT converge, instead oscillating between 1 and 2. The complement of the anti-Fibonacci sequence (numbers that ARE sums of two previous anti-Fibonacci numbers) has density 0. Test: compute A(n) for n up to 10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 approaches 1/4. Prove A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1) by induction. Impact: a beautiful counterpoint to the Fibonacci sequence — instead of converging to a constant, it grows quadratically while systematically avoiding addition.
directions.proof_strategy: Define A(1) = A(2) = 1, A(n+1) = smallest positive integer not equal to A(n) + A(n-1). Prove by strong induction: A(n) >= floor(n^2/4). Base: A(1)=1 >= 0, A(2)=1 >= 1. Inductive step: if A(k) >= floor(k^2/4) for k <= n, then A(n) + A(n-1) >= floor(n^2/4) + floor((n-1)^2/4), so A(n+1) <= A(n) + A(n-1) - 1 + delta where delta accounts for gaps, giving A(n+1) >= floor((n+1)^2/4). Prove A(n) <= ceil(n^2/4) + 1 by showing the avoidance constraint only blocks one value per step. Test: compute A(n) for n=1..10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 -> 1/4.
directions.title: The Anti-Fibonacci Sequence: Numbers That Avoid the Golden Ratio at All Costs

directions.description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.
directions.proof_strategy: Define an Escher staircase in ring R as a strictly ascending chain I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... such that intersection of I_n is contained in I_1. Prove Int(Z) has an Escher staircase: I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z}. Each I_n is strictly contained in I_{n+1} (the polynomial x choose n is in I_{n+1} but not I_n). Intersection of I_n = {0} contained in I_1. Prove k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n: the chain (x_1) contained in (x_1,x_2) contained in ... contained in (x_1,...,x_n) has length n. Prove Z_p has no Escher staircase (Noetherian). Test: verify for Int(Z) and k[x,y,z].
directions.title: Escher Staircases in Algebra: Infinite Ascending Chains That Loop Back

directions.description: Deja vu — the feeling that you've experienced something before — is a fixed point in a dynamical system. Model cognitive state as a function f: S -> S mapping current brain state to next brain state. A deja vu is a state s such that f^n(s) = s for some n > 0 — a periodic point of the cognitive dynamical system. Conjecture: By Sharkovsky's theorem, the existence of a period-3 orbit in the cognitive dynamics (three distinct states that cycle) implies chaos in the sense of Li-Yorke, meaning there exist uncountably many cognitive trajectories that are neither periodic nor convergent. Moreover, the set of deja vu states (periodic points of f) is dense in the cognitive state space S if f is continuous and S is an interval. The frequency of deja vu (occurring in ~70% of people) corresponds to the natural density of periodic points in a typical chaotic map. Test: model cognitive dynamics as a logistic map f(x) = rx(1-x) on [0,1] with parameter r chosen to match empirical deja vu frequencies. For r = 3.83 (period-3 window), compute the density of periodic points and compare to the 70% lifetime incidence. Impact: deja vu is not a glitch — it's a mathematical inevitability of continuous cognitive dynamics. Any continuous cognitive map with a period-3 orbit MUST have deja vu.
directions.proof_strategy: Model cognitive state space as S = [0,1] and cognitive dynamics as f: S -> S continuous. Apply Sharkovsky's theorem: if f has a point of period 3, then f has points of all periods. A deja vu state is a periodic point: s such that f^n(s) = s. Prove: the set of periodic points is dense in S for the logistic map at r = 3.83. Compute the density of periodic points: PeriodicPoints_n(f) / n approaches the topological entropy h(f) as n -> infinity. For the logistic map at r = 3.83, h(f) ~ 0.38. The lifetime incidence of deja vu (~70%) is consistent with the probability that a random orbit encounters a periodic point neighborhood within a typical observation window. Test: simulate 10000 random orbits of the logistic map and count how many encounter periodic neighborhoods.
directions.title: The Mathematics of Deja Vu: Fixed Points in Consciousness and Cognition

directions.description: We conjecture that for any prime p >= 3, integer base b >= 2 with p not dividing b, let l be the order of b modulo p and d = (p-1)/l. For each prime q dividing d let m_q be the exponent of q in d. Then there exist Dirichlet characters χ_{q,r} modulo p of order q^{m_q} (for 1 <= r <= m_q) such that the sum S of the repetend digits and the sum T of the squares of the digits satisfy S = (b-1)/2 * l + (b-1)/2 * Σ_{q|d} Σ_{r=1}^{m_q} [B_{χ_{q,r}}]_0, T = (T_0 + T_1)/d + Σ_{q|d} Σ_{r=2}^{m_q} [T_{q,r}]_0 / q^{m_q - r + 1} + [T_d]_0 / 2, where the definitions of T_0,T_1,T_{q,r} are the same as in Theorem 2 with the appropriate characters. Consequently the variance V_l = T/l - (S/l)^2 admits a closed formula involving only generalized Bernoulli numbers of characters whose order divides d. This recovers the known formulas for l = p-1 and l = (p-1)/2, and extends the theory to arbitrary repetend lengths dividing p-1.

directions.proof_strategy: The conjecture can be approached by viewing the digit sums S and T as exponential sums over the repetend and applying the theory of Dirichlet characters modulo p. Using the orthogonality relations we reduce S and T to sums of generalized Bernoulli numbers B_chi for characters chi whose order divides d. By induction on the number of distinct prime divisors of d, one can match the contributions of each prime power factor, reproducing the known formulas for powers of 2 and extending them to arbitrary d. A computational verification for many primes p <= 10000 and bases b <= 20 provides strong evidence for the conjecture. The final step is a formalisation in Lean 4, exploiting the existing DirichletCharacter and GeneralizedBernoulli frameworks in Mathlib.

Consequently any such unit palindrome of degree 4 must be associate either to a cyclotomic product or to 2·Φ₃(x)·(3x²−2x+3).

theorem unit_palindrome_degree4_classifies :
  ∀ (a b c : ℤ),
    let P := a*X^4 + b*X^3 + c*X^2 + b*X + a in
    (∀ z, eval P z = 0 → |z| = 1) →
      (∃ (k : ℤ) (hk : k ≠ 0), (P = k • (2 * (X^2 + X + 1) * (3*X^2 - 2*X + 3)) ∨
        (∃ (k : ℤ) (hk : k ≠ 0), (P = k • (X^2 + X + 1) * (X^2 + 1) ∨

The condition that all roots of P lie on |x|=1 is equivalent to Q having all real roots in [−2,2]. By analysing the integer parameters (a,b,c) we obtain finitely many possibilities for Q. A case‑by‑case discriminant analysis shows that the only admissible Q‑roots are u∈{−2,−1,0,1,2} (giving cyclotomic cases) and u=2/3. The latter yields P associate to 2·Φ₃(x)·(3x²−2x+3). Niven’s theorem rules out any other rational u in (−2,2) that could give a rational multiple of τ, so no further unit palindromes exist. directions.description: We conjecture that for any fixed escalation granularity m≥1, the misère P‑positions of the single‑theater escalation game (Definition 1) eventually follow a simple congruence modulo (m+1). Precisely, there exists an integer T(m) such that for every ladder length N≥T(m) and every remaining rung count r with 0≤ r≤ N, the position r is a P‑position under misère play if and only if r ≡ 0 (mod m+1). This strengthens Theorem 4.1 by asserting that the congruence holds for all sufficiently long ladders, not merely for the specific parameters considered in the paper.
domain_bridges: formal methods in combinatorial game theory

theorem misere_ladder_congruence_eventual (m : ℕ) (hm : m ≥ 1) : 
  ∃ (T : ℕ), ∀ (N : ℕ), N ≥ T → ∀ (r : ℕ), r ≤ N → 
    (is_P_position r) ↔ (r % (m + 1) = 0)
where
  is_P_position : ℕ → Prop := λ r =>
    match r with
    | 0 => false          -- r = 0 is an N‑position under misère
    | _ =>
      let opts := { d : ℕ | d ∈ escalation_set m ∧ d ≤ r } in
      ∀ d in opts, is_N_position (r - d)
and
  is_N_position : ℕ → Prop := λ r => r = 0 ∨ ∃ d in escalation_set m, d ≤ r ∧ is_P_position (r - d)
with
  escalation_set (m : ℕ) : Set ℕ := {1, 2, …, m}

directions.description: Let τ = (√5 + 1)/2 be the golden ratio. Specifically, S consists of algebraic numbers arising from the spectrum of certain infinite families of graphs constructed via recursive operations on Dynkin diagrams of types A_n and D_n, with gaps precisely at the transcendental values in (−T, T) \ S. This conjecture formalizes the claimed complete determination of limit points less than T, asserting that these limit points are exactly the accumulation points of spectra from specific graph-theoretic constructions.

Concretely, for each regular 4‑maniplex M its flag graph is a tetravalent graph in the census, and conversely every tetravalent graph G in the census determines a unique regular 4‑maniplex via its 1‑coskeleton. directions.description: The natural extension of the triangle map (a multi-dimensional continued fraction algorithm) admits a Z/2Z symmetry action generated by an involution τ corresponding to Young conjugation of integer partitions. This involution preserves the invariant measure on the natural extension space and permutes four distinguished subdomains D₁, D₂, D₃, D₄ into each other. Specifically, τ maps each subdomain to another in a 4-cycle or involution pattern, and each subdomain carries exactly 1/4 of the total measure. This symmetry generalizes the classical case for the Gauss map and Farey map, where Young conjugation provides a new perspective on previously known symmetries.

Equivalently, there exists a cyclic code of length (q^m+1)/2 and dimension n−1 that contains no full‑weight codeword, and no cyclically covering subspace of larger codimension can exist.

directions.description: The paper establishes a central limit theorem for Steinhaus random multiplicative functions in short intervals [x, x+y] for all y → ∞ with y = o(x), with a precise normalization that differs from √y when y is close to x. A natural conjecture is that the same result holds for Rademacher random multiplicative functions, at least for y in the range where the interval [x, x+y] contains a positive proportion of squarefree numbers (which is known to hold for y ≫ x^{1/2} unconditionally, and for all y → ∞ under RH). Specifically, for a Rademacher random multiplicative function f, and any y = y(x) with y → ∞, y = o(x), and such that the number of squarefree integers in [x, x+y] is (6/π²)y + o(y) with probability 1 - o(1), the normalized sum (1/σ(x,y)) ∑_{x≤n≤x+y} f(n) converges in distribution to N(0,1), where σ(x,y)² = Var(∑_{x≤n≤x+y} f(n)) has the same asymptotic as in the Steinhaus case.

directions.description:
Let \(F(Y,X_1,\dots,X_n)\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_1,\dots,X_n]\) be a strongly \(n\)-genuine polynomial whose generic Galois group over \(\mathbb{Q}(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) is a transitive subgroup \(G\le S_d\). Define
  \[\mathcal{S}(B)=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^n:\|\mathbf{x}\|_\infty\le B,\;\operatorname{Gal}(F(Y,\mathbf{x})/\mathbb{Q})\not\cong G\}.\]
  The conjecture asserts that \(\mathcal{S}(B)\) is contained in a thin set of type II and therefore satisfies the quantitative bound
  \[|\mathcal{S}(B)|\ll_{F,\varepsilon} B^{n-1+\varepsilon}\]
  for every \(\varepsilon>0\). In other words, for a strongly \(n\)-genuine polynomial the failure of Galois‑group preservation under specialization occurs only on a set of integer points of codimension at least one, with the expected power‑saving in the counting function. This statement is falsifiable: one can exhibit a concrete strongly \(n\)-genuine polynomial and compute (or bound) the number of exceptional specializations up to height \(B\).
domain_bridges: Galois Theory → Galois groups of specialized polynomials

import Mathlib.NumberTheory.ThinSet
import Mathlib.FieldTheory.Galois
import Mathlib.Data.Int.Pointwise

open Polynomial
open scoped BigOperators

/-- A polynomial `F : ℤ[Y, X₁, …, X_n]` is *strongly n‑genuine* if it satisfies the four equivalent
    characterisations from Bary-Soroker–Liu–Rouse.  For the purpose of this theorem we only need
    the quantitative control on the number of reducible specialisations given in
    `strongly_n_genuine.reducible_specialisations_bound`. -/
structure StronglyNGenuine (n : ℕ) (F : Polynomial (ℤ[X₁, …, X_n].succ)) where
  irreducible_generic : Irreducible (F.map (algebraMap ℤ ℚ))
  reducible_bound : ∀ B : ℕ,
    (Finset.filter (fun x : (Finset (ℤ) ^ n) =>
        (F.eval (Finset.unpair x)).IsReducible)) (Finset.Icc 0 B)).card ≤ C * B ^ (n-1)

/-- Let `F` be a strongly `n`‑genuine polynomial with generic Galois group `G`.  Then the set of
    integer specialisations `x : ℤ^n` with `‖x‖ ≤ B` for which the specialised Galois group is not
    isomorph
directions.proof_strategy: 1. Formalise the notion of a strongly n‑genuine polynomial in Lean using the four equivalent characterisations from the paper (e.g. control of reducible specialisations). 2. Show that the set of exceptional specialisations \(E\subset\mathbb{A}^n_{\mathbb{Q}}\) where the specialised Galois group differs from the generic one is a thin set of type II (no rational section). 3. Use the quantitative Hilbert‑Irreducibility theorem for thin sets already available in Mathlib (or import a recent formalisation) to obtain the bound \(O(B^{n-1+\varepsilon})\) for integer points of bounded height in a type II thin set. 4. Combine steps 1–3 to conclude the desired bound for \(\mathcal{S}(B)\). 5. Provide a concrete example (e.g. \(F(Y,X_1,X_2)=Y^3+X_1Y+X_2\)) and verify computationally that the bound holds for small \(B\), giving a test case that can falsify the conjecture.

The Ohsugi-Tsuchiya conjecture was verified for small graphs computationally; this conjecture asserts their computation was exhaustive up to dimension 35.

directions.description: We conjecture that the optimal lower bound for Hales‑Jewett numbers HJ(t,r) obtained from one‑weight colorings can be achieved by considering only diagonal lines (i.e., lines with a single active coordinate). Formally, let N_one(t,r) be the largest n for which there exists an integer weight vector w∈ ℤ^t such that the associated one‑weight coloring f_w : [t]^n → ℤ_r avoids monochromatic combinatorial lines. Let N_diag(t,r) be the largest n for which there exists a weight vector w such that f_w avoids monochromatic diagonal lines. The diagonal‑only conjecture asserts that N_one(t,r) = N_diag(t,r) for all t ≥ 2, r ≥ 1.
domain_bridges: Lean Mathlib formalization of van der Waerden numbers (combinatorial number theory)
Lean formalization of Hales‑Jewett theorem (project by Oliver Nash / Fabian Parliev)
Lean formalization of Gallai‑Witt theorem (by Johan Commelin)
Lean 4's support for dependent types and theorem proving suitable for encoding combinatorial structures
directions.proof_strategy: The conjecture can be approached by a combination of exhaustive search for small parameters (t ≤ 4, r ≤ 3) using SAT solvers to compute N_one and N_diag, and by constructing explicit weight vectors that achieve the bound for larger parameters based on solutions of Gallai homothety problems. A general proof would involve showing that any violation of the diagonal constraints yields a monochromatic line via combinatorial reasoning, possibly using the symmetric‑extremality results already proved in the paper.
directions.title: Diagonal-only conjecture for Hales‑Jewett numbers

directions.description: Let P be a finite poset. The main theorem shows that V₁(P) is an RB-domain iff P has a least element and its undirected Hasse graph is a tree. I conjecture that the four-point diamond (a poset with 4 elements where 2 incomparable elements are both below 2 incomparable maxima) is the unique minimal poset violating this: any finite poset P with fewer than 4 elements has V₁(P) an RB-domain, and among 4-element posets, only the four-point diamond violates the RB-domain property. This is falsifiable by either finding a smaller counterexample or proving no other 4-element poset violates the condition.

directions.proof_strategy: 1) Enumerate all finite posets with ≤3 elements and verify V₁(P) is always RB-domain using the known characterization. 2) Classify all 4-element posets and compute their undirected Hasse graphs. 3) Show that only the four-point diamond has both a least element and a cyclic Hasse graph (specifically, a 4-cycle). 4) Apply the local stochastic cone non-simpliciality argument to prove RB-domain failure for this case.
directions.title: Uniqueness of the Four-Point Diamond as Minimal RB-Domain Violator in Probabilistic Powerdomains

directions.description: Conjecture: Let (V,Q) be a non‑degenerate quadratic space over a finite field 𝔽_q with q>3 odd. Let Γ_Q be the connected component of the graph whose vertices are the non‑isotropic points of V and where two vertices are adjacent exactly when the line they span is a tangent line (i.e. contains a unique isotropic point). Then the full automorphism group of Γ_Q is isomorphic to the projective semi‑linear orthogonal group PΓO(V,Q).

Known results on the automorphism groups of tangent geometries (see Cuypers, Pasini) imply that this induced automorphism comes from an element of PΓO(V,Q). Conversely, verify that every element of PΓO(V,Q) preserves orthogonality and hence adjacency in Γ_Q, giving the reverse inclusion.
directions.title: Automorphism group of the orthogonal graph Γ_Q equals the projective semi‑linear orthogonal group

directions.description: For any abelian group G and any nonempty weight set Ψ ⊆ Hom(F,G) \ {0}, the weighted Davenport constant D_Ψ(G) equals the smallest positive integer n such that the union of kernels of all nonzero universal homomorphisms induced by n‑tuples from Ψ covers the Cartesian power F^n. In particular, D_Ψ(G) ≤ n iff F^n is covered by those kernels.

directions.description: We conjecture that for any torsion‑free CAT(0) group G, every unit in the group ring ℱ₂[ G ] whose support containsających at least three elements must in fact be trivial.  Equivalently, if x ∈ ℱ₂[ G ] is a unit and |supp(x)| > 2, then x equals ±1.  This statement is falsifiable: a single example of a nontrivial unit with support size ≥ 3 in a torsion‑free CAT(0) group would refute it, while a general proof would require showing that any such unit would give rise to a finite product structure satisfying orientability (𝕋₁), no‑fold (𝕋₂) and triple‑girth (𝕋₄), contradicting the obstruction proved in the referenced paper.
domain_bridges: Combinatorics – finite product structures and girth
Ring theory – units of group rings
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem no_nontrivial_units_gt2 (G : Type*) [Group G] [TorsionFree G] [CAT0 G] {x : F2[G]} (hx : IsUnit x) (hcard : x.support.card > 2) : False
directions.proof_strategy: Assume a nontrivial unit x ∈ ℱ₂[ G ] with |supp(x)| > 2.  Use the support sets of x and x⁻¹ to build a finite product structure Π of type (m,n) with m,n ≥ 2.  Show that Π must satisfy orientability (𝕋₁) and no‑fold (𝕋₂).  Then prove that the product identity forces Π to satisfy the triple‑girth condition (𝕋₄).  By the global girth obstruction theorem of Garg–Mineyev, this is impossible in a torsion‑free CAT(0) group, yielding a contradiction.  Thus no such unit can exist.
directions.title: Nontrivial Units with Large Support in F₂[ G ] for Torsion‑Free CAT(0) Groups

directions.description: Any simple graph on n vertices with minimum degree at least 3 that contains a Hamiltonian cycle must contain another cycle (a nontrivial cycle) of length at least n - c for some absolute constant c > 0. This formalizes the primary open conjecture addressed in the paper, which currently only has polynomial error bounds.

directions.proof_strategy: Formalize the definitions of Hamiltonian cycles, nontrivial cycles, and minimum degree in Lean. Then, adapt and combine the poset-based constructive methods with the nonconstructive lollipop argument (used for Smith's theorem and related results) to bound the error term by an absolute constant rather than O(n^{2/3}), likely requiring a novel combinatorial insight to overcome the paper's identified limitations of the current two methods.
directions.title: Girão-Kittipassorn-Narayanan Conjecture on Long Nontrivial Cycles

directions.description: For every integer k ≥ 6 with k ≡ 2 (mod 4), and for every pair of nonnegative integers (a, b) with a + b = k and a ≥ 1, the number 2^a · 3^b − 1 is composite. This formalizes the paper's theorem that row k of the principal skeleton L₁ contains no primes when k ≡ 2 (mod 4) and k ≥ 6. The proof exploits that k even forces a and b to share parity. When both even, 2^a · 3^b − 1 = (2^{a/2} · 3^{b/2} − 1)(2^{a/2} · 3^{b/2} + 1) via difference of squares, with both factors > 1 for k ≥ 6. When both odd, k ≡ 2 (mod 4) forces a ≡ b (mod 4), yielding 2^a · 3^b ≡ 1 (mod 5) so 5 | (2^a · 3^b − 1), and the cofactor exceeds 1 since k ≥ 6 excludes the case a = b = 1 where the value equals 5.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem row_k_mod4_eq2_no_primes (k a b : ℕ) (hk : k ≥ 6) (hk_mod : k % 4 = 2) (hab : a + b = k) (ha : a ≥ 1) : ¬Nat.Prime (2^a * 3^b - 1) := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Case split on parity of a and b. Since k ≡ 2 (mod 4) is even, a and b have the same parity. Case 1 (both even): apply difference of squares factorization 2^a · 3^b − 1 = (2^{a/2} · 3^{b/2} − 1)(2^{a/2} · 3^{b/2} + 1), verify both factors exceed 1 using k ≥ 6. Case 2 (both odd): from a + b ≡ 2 (mod 4) with a,b odd, deduce a ≡ b (mod 4); compute 2^a · 3^b mod 5 using 2^4 ≡ 3^4 ≡ 1 (mod 5) to show 5 | (2^a · 3^b − 1); verify 2^a · 3^b − 1 > 5 since k ≥ 6 excludes (a,b) = (1,1). Subsume b = 0 into Case 1 since then a = k is even.
directions.title: No primes in rows k ≡ 2 (mod 4) of the principal Collatz skeleton L₁

directions.description: For each n ≥ 1, the map φ_n from the degree-n graded piece of the cone algebra on ℚⁿ to the (n−1)-chains of the ind-triangulation of S^{n−1} at all rational rays, defined on linearly independent tuples (v₁,…,vₙ) by φ_n([C(v₁,…,vₙ)]) = sgn(det(v₁,…,vₙ)) · Δ(ℚv₁,…,ℚvₙ), extends to a GL_n(ℚ)-equivariant isomorphism of ℚ-modules. This identifies the top-degree cone algebra graded piece with the spherical chain module computing H_{n−1}(S^{n−1}; ℚ).
directions.proof_strategy: Define the cone algebra with its degree filtration and construct the spherical chain complex C(n) from rational rays with the stellar subdivision presentation. Verify well-definedness of φ_n by checking it respects the relations on both sides (stellar subdivision on the chain side, additivity on the cone side). Prove equivariance by direct computation of the GL_n(ℚ)-action on both sides. Establish bijectivity by constructing an explicit inverse using the presentation of C(n)_{n-1} and the identification of simplicial cones with oriented intersections of half-spaces.
directions.title: GL_n-equivariant isomorphism between graded cone algebra and spherical chains

directions.description: The transformation matrix encoding the change of the h-vector of a simplicial complex under the r-colored barycentric subdivision is totally positive (all minors are non-negative). The paper establishes that this matrix is TP_2, and this conjecture posits that the stronger total positivity (TP) property holds, extending the confirmed TP property of the standard barycentric and interval subdivisions.

This may involve verifying the Whitney conditions or finding a suitable planar network whose path-generating function equals the transformation matrix entries.
directions.title: Total positivity of the r-colored barycentric subdivision transformation matrix

directions.description: For an odd prime p, let n = (p-1)/2 and χ be the Legendre symbol modulo p. For a ∈ F_p^×, define D_a(0) = det_{1 ≤ i,j ≤ n}(χ(i^2 - a*j)). Then D_a(0) = 0 if and only if p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and χ(a * n!) = 1.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the Legendre symbol and the matrix M over the integers. Show that the determinant of M vanishes under the stated conditions by applying row and column operations to relate the determinant to the Pfaffian of an associated skew-symmetric matrix, leveraging properties of quadratic residues modulo p.
directions.title: Vanishing Criterion for Legendre Symbol Determinants

directions.description: For any connected trivalent ribbon graph G embedded on a closed surface, the degree-zero Penrose homology group H^{0,*}(G) at the specialization λ = 3 is nonzero if and only if G admits a proper 3-edge coloring (Tait coloring). This refines the classical Penrose criterion—which states P(G;3) > 0 iff G is Tait-colorable—by identifying the specific homological degree that detects colorability, analogous to how Khovanov homology detects the unknot in degree zero.

directions.proof_strategy: Forward direction: For each Tait coloring c of G, construct an explicit generator of H^{0,*}(G) using the state-sum structure of the Penrose homology cube of resolutions, ensuring distinct colorings yield linearly independent classes. Reverse direction: Show that any nonzero class in H^{0,*}(G) forces the existence of a Tait coloring by analyzing the cobordism maps in the TQFT-valued chain complex and proving that non-colorable graphs have vanishing H^{0,*}. The nonorientable cobordism framework is essential for handling the sign assignments that distinguish colorable from non-colorable configurations.
directions.title: Penrose Homology Detects Tait Colorability

That is, α(G) ≥ (a(G) + res(G)) / Δ(G), or equivalently, α(G) * Δ(G) ≥ a(G) + res(G).

  sorry

Construct annihilating decompositions and prove the edge count inequality e(A) ≤ e(B) for the partition. Combine this with the classical Havel-Hakimi residue inequality res(G) ≤ α(G) and the Caro-Wei bounds to establish the multiplicative inequality.

directions.description: For all positive integers m and n, the number of intervals in the greedy m-Tamari poset on m-Dyck paths of semi-length n equals the number of rooted planar (m+1)-constellations with n black faces. This generalizes the m=1 case proven in the paper (where greedy Tamari intervals are equinumerous to bipartite planar maps, i.e., 2-constellations) and remains open for m ≥ 2.

  sorry

For general m, one would need to: (1) formalize m-Dyck paths and the greedy m-Tamari poset cover relation; (2) define planar (m+1)-constellations; (3) establish that both families satisfy isomorphic recursive decomposition schemes; (4) conclude equinumerosity by induction. The refined conjecture additionally tracks the number of vertices of degree m+1 in the constellation and the number of ascents of the lower bound of the interval.
directions.title: Equinumerosity of greedy m-Tamari intervals and planar (m+1)-constellations

directions.description: For any prime p, the Markov chain on ℕ defined by the Klagsbrun-Mazur-Rubin twist process for p-Selmer ranks of even-dimensional Galois modules satisfying the KMR technical conditions is irreducible, aperiodic, and positive recurrent. Its unique stationary distribution π assigns strictly positive probability to every rank r ∈ ℕ, and the distribution of p-Selmer ranks in the twist family ordered by the product of ramified primes converges to π.

(π : ℕ → ℝ), IsStationaryDistribution (kmrChain p M) π ∧ (∀ r, 0 < π r) ∧ ∀ r₀, Tendsto (fun n => (kmrChain p M)^n r₀) atTop (π)

directions.description: The paper proves an edge-spectral supersaturation bound with a sharp constant $B_F$ for color-critical graphs $F$ with $\chi(F) \ge 4$. A natural open problem is whether the same bound holds for $\chi(F) = 3$, most notably for triangles ($K_3$). The conjecture states that for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exist $\delta > 0$ and $M$ such that for all $m \ge M$ and $0 < q \le \delta \sqrt{m}$, any graph $G$ with $m$ edges and $\lambda^2(G) \ge m + q$ contains at least $(1 - \epsilon) q \sqrt{m}$ triangles, corresponding to the sharp constant $B_{K_3} = 1$.

  ∃ (δ : ℝ) (M : ℕ) (hδ : δ > 0), ∀ (m : ℕ) (q : ℝ) (G : SimpleGraph ℕ),
  m ≥ M → 0 < q → q ≤ δ * Real.sqrt m → G.edgeFinset.card = m →
  (adjSpectralRadius G)^2 ≥ m + q →

  sorry

This requires establishing spectral stability for near-bipartite graphs, then applying supersaturation counting arguments within the bipartite structure to find the requisite number of triangles. The bipartite case $r=2$ might require different spectral inequalities or combinatorial reductions since the Li-Liu-Zhang bound was only for $r \ge 3$.
directions.title: Edge-Spectral Supersaturation for Triangles

Prove the equivalence between the seating problem and the graph decomposition problem (Theorem 3.2). Establish base cases by formalizing Lemma 3.3 (for odd m) and Lemma 3.4 (for even m). Construct the general solution by inductively building decompositions for larger n by extending the graph using 1-regular subgraph decompositions (Lemma 3.5 and Lemma 3.6).

directions.description: For every finite poset P of width at most 2, the Ehrhart h*-polynomial h*(O(P); t) of the order polytope O(P) is real-rooted. This extends the paper's result for generalized snake posets (a proper subclass of width-two posets) to all width-two posets, and would unify real-rootedness phenomena observed across flow polytopes, rook polynomials, and P-Eulerian polynomials for this entire width regime.

    (P : Finset α) (h_width : (maxAntichain P).card ≤ 2) :
    (hStarPoly (orderPolytope P)).RealRooted :=
  by
    sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Decompose an arbitrary width-two poset into a union of chains and analyze how its Jordan-Hölder set and P-Eulerian polynomial relate to a generalized non-nesting rook polynomial on an associated Ferrers diagram. The key obstacle is that arbitrary width-two posets need not be generalized snake posets, so the existing rook polynomial correspondence must be extended to handle arbitrary interleavings of two chains, possibly via interlacing root arguments or real-rootedness-preserving operations on the associated generating polynomials.
directions.title: Real-rootedness of h*-polynomials for width-two order polytopes

directions.description: The paper establishes the upper bound $f_{F,G}(n) \le C(\log n)^{\beta_F}$ for $r$-uniform hypergraphs. This conjecture proposes that this bound is asymptotically tight, meaning there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that $f_{F,G}(n) \ge c(\log n)^{\beta_F}$ for any non-empty $r$-graph $F$ and $2$-tightly connected $r$-graph $G$ with no homomorphism from $G$ to $F$, thereby completely determining the polylogarithmic exponent $\beta_F$.

import Mathlib.Data.Real.Basic

-- Placeholder definitions for r-uniform hypergraphs and related concepts
variable {r : ℕ}

structure RUniformHypergraph where
  vertices : Finset ℕ
  edges : Finset (Finset ℕ)
  uniform : ∀ e ∈ edges, e.card = r
  subset : ∀ e ∈ edges, e ⊆ vertices

-- f_{F,G}(n) is the maximum size of an induced F-free subgraph in any n-vertex G-free r-graph
-- beta_F is the maximum of e(P)/(v(P)-1) over non-empty subgraphs P of the 2-shadow of F

theorem generalized_erdos_rogers_lower_bound (r : ℕ) (hr : r ≥ 3)
    (F : RUniformHypergraph) (hF : F.edges.Nonempty)

    (hNoHom : ¬∃ φ, is_homomorphism φ G F) :

      f_F_G F G n ≥ c * (Real.log n) ^ (beta_F F) :=

The analysis would require establishing isoperimetric inequalities on the 2-shadow $\partial_2F$ to demonstrate that any large enough induced subgraph must contain a copy of $F$, yielding the matching lower bound.

directions.description: For integers n, k, t with n >= 3 and 0 <= k <= n-3, any n-vertex graph that is not k-edge Hamiltonian contains at most max(g_t(n, k, 1), g_t(n, k, floor((n-1-k)/2))) t-stars, where g_t(n, k, i) = i * choose(i+k, t) + (n-2*i-k) * choose(n-i-1, t) + (i+k) * choose(n-1, t). This corresponds to the extremal graphs G(n, k, 1) and G(n, k, i_0).
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Choose.Basic

variable {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (k t : ℕ)

-- A linear forest is a disjoint union of paths. We omit the full formalization for brevity.
-- A graph is k-edge Hamiltonian if every linear forest with at most k edges is contained in a Hamilton cycle.
def IsKEdgeHamiltonian : Prop :=
  ∀ F : SimpleGraph (Fin n), IsLinearForest F ∧ F.edgeFinset.card ≤ k → 
    ∃ (p : List (Fin n)), p.IsHamiltonCycle G ∧ ...

-- The number of t-stars in a graph, counting subgraphs isomorphic to K_{1,t}
def starCount : ℕ :=
  Finset.sum Finset.univ fun v => Nat.choose (G.degree v) t

-- The function g_t(n, ℓ, i)
def g_t (n ℓ i t : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  i * Nat.choose (i + ℓ) t + (n - 2 * i - ℓ) * Nat.choose (n - i - 1) t + (i + ℓ) * Nat.choose (n - 1) t

theorem max_stars_not_k_edge_hamiltonian 
    (hk : k ≤ n - 3) 
    (hG : ¬ IsKEdgeHamiltonian G k) :
    starCount G t ≤ max (g_t n k 1 t) (g_t n k ((n - 1 - k) / 2) t) := b
directions.proof_strategy: Induction on the number of vertices or edges, combined with structural graph theory techniques such as vertex deletion and edge shifting, reducing the problem to analyzing the specific extremal graphs G(n, k, 1) and G(n, k, i_0).
directions.title: Conjecture on the Maximum Number of Stars in Non-k-Edge-Hamiltonian Graphs

directions.description: The minimal absolute value σ₅(n) of a non-vanishing sum of n fifth roots of unity is monotone non-increasing over congruence classes of n modulo 5. Furthermore, a strict decrease σ₅(n) > σ₅(n+5) occurs if and only if n+5 is of the form 5Fₘ, Lₘ, or 2Lₘ for some positive integer m, where Fₘ and Lₘ denote the m-th Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, respectively.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
import Mathlib.NumberTheory.RootsOfUnity
import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Fib
import Mathlib.Analysis.Complex.Basic

open Complex

/-- A sum of n 5th roots of unity -/
def isFifthRootSum (n : ℕ) (s : ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ a : Fin 5 → ℕ, (∑ i, (a i : ℂ)) = n ∧ 
    s = a 0 + (a 1) * exp (2 * π * I / 5) + (a 2) * exp (4 * π * I / 5) + 
        (a 3) * exp (6 * π * I / 5) + (a 4) * exp (8 * π * I / 5)

/-- The minimal absolute value of a non-vanishing sum of n 5th roots of unity -/
def sigma_5 (n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  sInf { r : ℝ | ∃ s, isFifthRootSum n s ∧ s ≠ 0 ∧ r = ‖s‖ }

/-- Lucas numbers -/
def lucas : ℕ → ℕ
  | 0 => 2
  | 1 => 1
  | n + 2 => lucas n + lucas (n + 1)

theorem sigma_5_monotone_and_jumps (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) :
    sigma_5 n ≥ sigma_5 (n + 5) ∧
    (sigma_5 n > sigma_5 (n + 5) ↔ 
      ∃ m, n + 5 = 5 * Nat.fib m ∨ n + 5 = lucas m ∨ n + 5 = 2 * lucas m) := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Define the function σ₅(n) as the infimum of the absolute values of non-vanishing sums of n 5th roots of unity. Prove the monotonicity within congruence classes modulo 5 by constructing appropriate sums. Characterize the strict decreases by relating the problem to rational approximations of the golden ratio via continued fractions, using the specific properties of Fibonacci and Lucas numbers.
directions.title: Monotonicity and Jumps of Minimal Absolute Values of Fifth Roots of Unity Sums

directions.description: For every positive integer k, there exist infinitely many odd integers s such that the 5-rank of the Pólya group Po(K_s) of the Lecacheux quintic field K_s equals k. This strengthens the paper's result from '5-rank at least k for a set of positive density' to '5-rank exactly k for infinitely many parameters', providing a complete stratification of achievable 5-ranks in this family.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem polya_five_rank_exact_realization (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) : {s : ℤ | Odd s ∧ (fiveRank (PolyaGroup (LecacheuxQuintic s))) = k}.Infinite

For each target rank k, use the parametric structure of Lecacheux fields to identify congruence conditions on s that control which prime ideals above 5 generate the characteristic ideals. Show that the conditions for achieving rank exactly k (rather than at least k) are satisfied for infinitely many s by applying Chebotarev's density theorem in the cyclotomic field Q(ζ₅) and its subfields. The key step is excluding 'excess rank' contributions by ensuring that only k of the possible 5-adic prime ideals contribute non-trivially to the Pólya group, which can be achieved by imposing suitable splitting conditions on s.
directions.title: Exact 5-Rank Realization for Pólya Groups of Lecacheux Quintic Fields

directions.description: For the morphisms $\phi$ (where $\phi(a)=abc, \phi(b)=ac, \phi(c)=b$) and $\mu$ (where $\mu(a)=a, \mu(b)=b, \mu(c)=cbbbc$), let $x'_k = \phi^k(a)$ and $x_k = \mu(x'_k)$. The conjecture states that for any $k \ge 0$, if a $3^+$-parameterized square $w = uv$ with $|u|=|v| \ge 3$ exists as a subword of $x_k$, then $u=v$, meaning there are no non-standard $3^+$-parameterized squares.

Prove that any parameterized square of length $\ge 6$ in $x_k$ implies $u=v$ by analyzing the local structure around occurrences of 'c' and 'bb', leveraging the fact that $x'_k$ is square-free and the specific substitution properties of $\mu$.

directions.description: The regularized coupling of two vector-valued weight 3/2 mock Eisenstein series (which individually yield depth one mock modular forms) produces a depth two mock modular form of weight 3. Specifically, the completion of this coupled object satisfies a $\bar{\partial}$-equation whose shadow is a linear combination of tensor products of depth one mock Eisenstein series and holomorphic modular forms.

Compute the Fourier expansion of the coupled series and verify its $\bar{\partial}$-equation using the known analytic properties of mock Eisenstein series and Rankin-Selberg integrals.
directions.title: Depth Two Mock Modularity of Coupled Mock Eisenstein Series

directions.description: Within the class of distance-hereditary graphs, balanced graphs coincide exactly with hereditary clique-Helly graphs, and equivalently with graphs forbidding the complement of 3K₂ as an induced subgraph. This conjecture formalizes the main theorem of the paper: for every distance-hereditary graph G, G is balanced if and only if G contains no induced copy of 3K₂ (the complement of three disjoint edges, i.e., the graph on six vertices partitioned into three independent edges, complemented).

theorem balanced_iff_no_induced_3K2_bar_of_distance_hereditary {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (h_dh : DistanceHereditary G) : Balanced G ↔ ¬ HasInducedSubgraph G (complement (disjointUnionOf 3 (edgeGraph : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)))) := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Formalize the three key definitions (distance-hereditary, balanced via clique-matrix condition, hereditary clique-Helly) and the graph 3K₂-bar. Prove the equivalence in two directions: (1) If a distance-hereditary graph G is balanced, it contains no induced 3K₂-bar (using the known result that balanced implies no extended odd sun, and that 3K₂-bar is an extended odd sun within distance-hereditary graphs). (2) If a distance-hereditary graph G contains no induced 3K₂-bar, then it is hereditary clique-Helly and hence balanced. The key structural lemma is that within distance-hereditary graphs, the only minimal obstruction to balancedness that is also an extended odd sun is 3K₂-bar. Decompose the proof using the pruning-sequence characterization of distance-hereditary graphs to handle each attachment operation (twin, pendant) inductively.
directions.title: Balanced equals hereditary clique-Helly within distance-hereditary graphs

directions.description: In type A_n, the subalgebra B_aff of the affine Hecke algebra admits a canonical basis {b_{W_fin w}} indexed by cosets W_fin \ W_aff. The conjecture states that the structure constants of B_aff with respect to this canonical basis are polynomials in v with non-negative integer coefficients: for any two cosets W_fin w and W_fin w' in W_fin \ W_aff, the product b_{W_fin w} · b_{W_fin w'} = Σ c_{w,w'}^z · b_{W_fin z} where each c_{w,w'}^z ∈ Z_{≥0}[v]. This is the v-deformed analogue of the positivity of structure constants in the affine Fomin-Stanley subalgebra (equivalently, homology of the affine Grassmannian).

directions.proof_strategy: First formalize the affine Weyl group W_aff = W_fin ⋉ Q∨ in type A_n as a Coxeter group with generators S_aff = S_fin ∪ {s_0}. Define the affine Hecke algebra H_aff over Z[v,v^{-1}] with Bernstein presentation and quadratic relations. Construct the pseudo-centralizer subalgebra B_aff as the subalgebra generated by appropriate elements arising from the DAHA centralizer construction. Prove the canonical basis exists (indexed by W_fin \ W_aff) by establishing a graded module structure and applying the bar-involution argument. Finally, establish positivity of structure constants using geometric arguments via the affine Grassmannian or combinatorial arguments via the v-deformed Pieri rule.
directions.title: Positivity of structure constants for the canonical basis of the pseudo-centralizer subalgebra in type A

directions.description: The oriented chromatic number of the directed Cartesian product C⃗₃ □ C⃗₄ of directed 3- and 4-cycles equals 7. That is, there exists a digraph homomorphism from C⃗₃ □ C⃗₄ to some 7-vertex tournament, but no digraph homomorphism from C⃗₃ □ C⃣₄ to any 6-vertex tournament. This finite combinatorial fact is the essential obstruction in the proof that the continuous oriented chromatic number of the directed Schreier graph F⃗(2^ℤ²) is 7: the torus tile C₃ □ C₄ is one of the Twelve Tiles, and ruling out 6-vertex tournaments as targets for this tile (along with the long tile) constitutes the core of the lower bound argument.

    orientedChromaticNumber (directedCartesianProduct (directedCycle 3) (directedCycle 4)) = 7 := by
  sorry

For the upper bound, explicitly construct a homomorphism to a 7-vertex tournament by assigning colors to each of the 12 vertices. For the lower bound, enumerate all 35 non-isomorphic strong tournaments on 6 vertices and verify that none admits a homomorphism from C⃗₃ □ C⃗₄. The 27 tournaments handled by order-energy and 4 by non-order energies yield to algebraic invariants formalizable as homomorphism obstructions; the remaining 4 require the diagonal marker propagation argument exploiting gcd(3,4)=1, which forces marker-set invariance under translation by 4 in Z/3Z—a contradiction for proper nonempty sets.
directions.title: Oriented chromatic number of the directed torus C₃ □ C₄

directions.description: For integers n > l ≥ 2, if E ⊆ ℝⁿ is a Borel set with Hausdorff dimension dim_H(E) > l+1, then for almost every V ∈ G(n,l), the orthogonal projection Π_V(E) has nonempty interior. This improves the Peres–Schlag exponent 2l to l+1, matching the sharp finite-field threshold established in the paper. The case l=1 is excluded since 2l = l+1 = 2 is already sharp by Besicovitch–Mattila constructions. For l ≥ 2, the gap between the known bound 2l and the conjectured bound l+1 remains open, and the paper's finite-field result strongly suggests l+1 is the true threshold.

theorem peres_schlag_sharp_threshold {n l : ℕ} (hl : 2 ≤ l) (hl₂ : l < n)
    {E : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))} (hE : IsBorel E)
    (hdim : hausdorffDim E > (l + 1 : ℝ)) :
    ∀ᵐ V ∂(grassmannMeasure n l),
      (interior (orthogonalProjection V '' E)).Nonempty := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: The finite-field proof shows the l+1 threshold arises from polynomial method arguments linked to Kakeya set bounds. To lift this to ℝⁿ: (1) discretize the Euclidean problem by replacing E with a δ-packing and passing to a finite-field model via rescaling and reduction mod p, (2) apply the finite-field sharp threshold result to obtain rich projections for the discretized set, (3) use Bourgain's framework reformulating Peres–Schlag in terms of L² bounds for maximal k-plane transforms controlled by Riesz energy, (4) combine with the best available Kakeya maximal L^p estimates (from BCCLXZ and related works) and the paper's maximal k-plane transform bounds to close the gap from 2l down to l+1. Guth's polynomial partitioning method may provide the continuous analogue of the polynomial method used in the finite-field setting.
directions.title: Sharp Euclidean Peres–Schlag Threshold Equals l+1 for l ≥ 2

directions.description: We conjecture that for each integer n≥3 the exponent 3/(2n‑1) in the finite‑field Peres‑Schlag theorem for product sets is optimal. More precisely, there exists a constant c_n > 0 such that for all sufficiently large primes p there is a subset A ⊂ ℤ_p with |A| ≤ c_n·p^{3/(2n‑1)} for which no choice of coefficients t_1,…,t_n ∈ ℤ_p yields a covering t_1A + … + t_nA = ℤ_p. Equivalently, the threshold cannot be lowered below 3/(2n‑1).
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem peres_schlag_sharp (n : Nat) (hn : 3 <= n) : 
  forall (p : Nat) [hp : Prime p],
    exists (c : Q), (0 < c) /
      forall (A : Finset (Zmod p)),
        (A.card <= c * (p : Q) ^ (3/(2*n - 1 : Q))) ->
          not (exists (t : Fin n -> Zmod p), forall (x : Zmod p), x ∈ (t 0).smul A + … + (t (n-1)).smul A)
directions.proof_strategy: To prove the conjecture one would construct, for each n, small subsets A ⊂ ℤ_p (for large p) that avoid being covered by any n‑term dilated sum. This would likely involve adapting known Kakeya‑type or cap‑set constructions to produce sets whose n‑fold linear images have small density. A successful construction would establish the sharpness of the exponent 3/(2n‑1). A disproof would require showing that any set of size ≈ p^{3/(2n‑1)} inevitably yields a covering, perhaps via Fourier‑analytic or algebraic‑geometric methods.
directions.title: Sharpness of the finite‑field Peres‑Schlag exponent for product sets

directions.description: Any finite group that can be expressed as the product of two dihedral subgroups is solvable. This extends the classical result of Kegel and Wielandt on the solvability of products of two nilpotent groups to the case of dihedral groups, noting that dihedral groups are solvable (specifically, metacyclic) but not necessarily nilpotent.

import Mathlib.GroupTheory.Solvable

/-- A subgroup is dihedral if it is isomorphic to a finite dihedral group. -/
def IsDihedral {G : Type*} [Group G] (H : Subgroup G) : Prop :=
  ∃ n : Nat, 0 < n ∧ Nonempty (H ≃* DihedralGroup n)

/-- A group is bidihedral if it is the product of two dihedral subgroups. -/
def IsBidihedral (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ (A B : Subgroup G), A * B = ⊤ ∧ IsDihedral A ∧ IsDihedral B

/-- Any finite bidihedral group is solvable. -/
theorem finite_bidihedral_is_solvable (G : Type*) [Group G] [Fintype G] :
    IsBidihedral G → IsSolvable G := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Assume the group is non-solvable and consider a minimal counterexample, which must be an almost simple group. Then apply the classification of exact factorizations of almost simple groups (Li, Wang, Xia) and maximal factorizations (Liebeck, Praeger, Saxl) to show that no almost simple group can be factorized as a product of two dihedral subgroups, yielding a contradiction.
directions.title: Solvability of Finite Bidihedral Groups

directions.description: Every admissible graph (a graph with no pendant path of length two, i.e., no path x-y-z with d(x)=1 and d(y)=2) admits a strong majority edge-coloring with at most 4 colors. A strong majority edge-coloring requires that for every edge e=uv and every color i, at most (d(u)+d(v))/2 - 1 edges adjacent to e receive color i. Kalinowski, Kamyczura, Pilśniak, and Woźniak originally proved 8 colors suffice and conjectured 4; the current paper improves the bound to 5, but the conjecture remains open.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
variable {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
variable (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- A graph is admissible if it contains no pendant path of length two
    (no path x-y-z with d(x) = 1 and d(y) = 2). -/
def IsAdmissible : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃x y z : V⦄, G.Adj x y → G.Adj y z → G.degree x ≠ 1 ∨ G.degree y ≠ 2

/-- A strong majority edge-coloring with ≤ 4 colors: for every edge e = uv
    and color i, at most half the adjacent edges share color i:
    |{f adjacent to e : c(f) = i}| ≤ (d(u) + d(v)) / 2 - 1 -/
def IsStrongMajorityEdgeColoring (c : G.Edge → Fin 4) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃e : G.Edge⦄ ⦃i : Fin 4⦄,
    Finset.card (Finset.filter (fun f =>

directions.description: For the elliptic curve E_7: y^2 = x^3 + 49/4 over the rational numbers, let P_7 = (84, 756) be the rational point corresponding to the cube sum 2^3 + (-1)^3 = 7. The explicit Gross-Zagier formula from Yin's paper implies that L'(E_7, 1) / Omega_7 = (1/2) * hat_h_Q(P_7), where Omega_7 is the real Neron period of E_7 and hat_h_Q is the Neron-Tate height over Q.

directions.description: The shifted $t$-Schur function $\mathcal{Q}_\lambda(X;t)$, generated by the modified odd Greaves--Jing--Zhu operator $\mathcal{Y}_t(z) = \mathcal{R}_t \Phi(z) \mathcal{R}_t^{-1}$ (where $\mathcal{R}_t$ rescales each odd power sum $p_n \mapsto (1-t^n)p_n$ and $\Phi(z)$ is the classical Schur $Q$ vertex operator), equals the classical Schur $Q$-function $Q_\lambda$ under the plethystic substitution $X \mapsto X - tX$. Equivalently, $\mathcal{R}_t Q_\lambda(X) = Q_\lambda[X - tX]$ for every strict partition $\lambda$ and formal parameter $t$. This encapsulates the conjugation relation and the resulting plethystic interpretation of the modified operator's spectrum.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem shifted_t_schur_plethystic_identity
    {R : Type*} [CommRing R] [IsDomain R]
    (λ : StrictPartition) (t : R) :
    shiftedTSchur λ t =
      schurQ λ (plethysticSubst (fun ω => ω - t • ω) oddPowerSumAlgebra) := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: First formalize the odd power-sum ring $\Gamma_t = \mathbb{Q}(t)[p_1, p_3, p_5, \ldots]$ as a graded Hopf algebra over $\mathbb{Q}(t)$. Define the diagonal automorphism $\mathcal{R}_t$ rescaling $p_n \mapsto (1-t^n)p_n$ for odd $n$, and prove it is a Hopf algebra automorphism. Define the classical Schur $Q$ vertex operator $\Phi(z)$ via its exponential form in creation/annihilation operators on $\Gamma_t$. Construct the modified operator $\mathcal{Y}_t(z)$ and prove the conjugation identity $\mathcal{Y}_t(z) = \mathcal{R}_t \Phi(z) \mathcal{R}_t^{-1}$ by verifying that $\mathcal{R}_t p_n \mathcal{R}_t^{-1} = (1-t^n)p_n$ and $\mathcal{R}_t (\partial/p_n) \mathcal{R}_t^{-1} = (1-t^n)^{-1} \partial/p_n$. The plethystic identity then follows by applying both sides to the vacuum vector and extracting coefficients indexed by strict partitions, using that $\mathcal{R}_t^{-1}|0\rangle = |0\rangle$.
directions.title: Shifted t-Schur plethystic identity via modified odd operator conjugation

directions.description: The paper proves, assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), that if K is a totally real Galois number field of degree n ≥ 3 and p is an odd rational prime which does not split completely in K, then every generating set of the ray class group Cl_K^{(p)^N} with modulus (p)^N is a Euclidean system. This conjecture posits that the GRH assumption can be removed, asserting that the statement holds unconditionally.

-- Conjecture: Unconditional Euclidean Systems for Ray Classes
theorem unconditional_euclidean_system_ray_class 
    {K : Type*} [Field K] [NumberField K]
    [IsGalois K ℚ] [IsTotallyReal K] 
    (h_deg : FiniteDimensional.finrank K ℚ ≥ 3)
    (p : ℕ) (hp : Nat.Prime p) (hp_odd : Odd p) 
    (h_not_split : ¬ SplitsCompletely p (𝓞 K))
    {N : ℕ} (hN : 0 < N)
    (C : Set (RayClassGroup K (Ideal.map (algebraMap ℤ (𝓞 K)) (Ideal.span {(p : ℤ)}) ^ N)))
    (h_gen : GeneratesRayClassGroup C) :
    IsEuclideanSystemOfRayClasses C := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: The existing proof relies on GRH via Artin's generalized primitive root conjecture to guarantee the existence of primes with specific norm properties that enable the Euclidean division. An unconditional proof would likely require circumventing GRH by developing new analytic number theory techniques to establish stronger lower bounds on the relevant prime counting functions, or by discovering an alternative algebraic mechanism for constructing the Euclidean norm function for ray classes.
directions.title: Unconditional Euclidean Systems for Ray Classes in Totally Real Galois Fields

directions.description: For every n ≥ 0, the n-th row generating function of the square of the Eulerian triangle—defined as the polynomial ∑_k (∑_j A(n,j)·A(j,k)) x^k where A(n,k) is the Eulerian number counting permutations of [n] with k descents—has only real roots. This extends the paper's results on powers of Pascal, Stirling, and Narayana triangles to the still-open Eulerian case.

def eulerian (n k : ℕ) : ℕ := sorry

def eulerianSquare (n k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), eulerian n j * eulerian j k

def eulerianSquareRGF (n : ℕ) : Polynomial ℝ :=
  ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (eulerianSquare n k : ℝ) • Polynomial.X ^ k

    ∀ z : ℂ, (eulerianSquareRGF n).IsRoot z → z.im = 0 := by
  sorry
